query: A media startup is launching a professional networking app where members connect, follow companies, and browse personalized activity streams. The team needs a data store that models highly connected relationships among people, follows, and posts while supporting horizontal scale for rapid growth to tens of millions of users. Which kind of database technology should they choose?

options.text: Cloud Spanner
options.explanation: A globally distributed relational database that provides strong consistency and horizontal scaling with SQL capabilities

options.text: Document oriented NoSQL database
options.explanation: A store for flexible JSON like documents that works well when records have varying fields and schema evolution is frequent

options.text: Graph NoSQL database engine
options.explanation: A database that models entities as nodes and relationships as edges to enable efficient traversal of interconnected data

options.text: Key value NoSQL database
options.explanation: A store optimized for simple key based access that delivers very fast reads and writes for individual items

answer:
The correct option is Graph NoSQL database engine.

A graph database models entities as nodes and their relationships as edges, which aligns directly with people, follow relationships, companies, and posts. Features like efficient multi hop traversals and adjacency queries make a graph database ideal for building feeds, recommendations, and mutual connection discovery. Many graph databases are designed for horizontal scale by distributing storage and computation across clusters, which supports rapid growth to tens of millions of users.

Cloud Spanner offers global relational consistency and strong scaling yet it is optimized for normalized relational schemas and SQL rather than pointer heavy traversals and repeated relationship hops. Modeling graph queries in SQL can be complex and inefficient for this use case.

Document oriented NoSQL database works well for flexible document schemas and hierarchical data but it does not natively store or traverse relationships efficiently across many documents. Multi hop queries and graph style recommendations often require heavy denormalization and application side joins.

Key value NoSQL database excels at simple lookups with very high throughput yet it lacks native graph structures and efficient traversal across connected entities. Implementing friend of friend and feed expansion logic becomes application heavy and inefficient.

A. Document NoSQL Database
B. Column-family NoSQL Database
C. Graph NoSQL Database

tip: Map the access pattern to the data model. When you see highly connected data and repeated traversals think graph. When you see flexible JSON and hierarchical records think document. When you see simple lookups at massive scale think key value. When you see strong relational consistency and SQL at global scale think Spanner.

query: You operate the online ticketing platform for scrumtuous.com and you use Cloud Spanner to store orders. During a high profile concert on sale the Cloud Spanner instance entered a maintenance event and the service was unavailable for more than 12 minutes which triggered customer escalations. You must take immediate action to stop unplanned maintenance from interrupting production during critical periods. What should you do?

options.text: Upgrade the Cloud Spanner instance to a multi region configuration to avoid maintenance impact
options.explanation: A multi region configuration increases availability by replicating data across regions

options.text: Configure a maintenance exclusion window on the Cloud Spanner instance during peak sales hours
options.explanation: A maintenance exclusion defines a time range when Google Cloud does not start maintenance for the managed service

options.text: Open a Support case to investigate why the instance was down for more than 12 minutes
options.explanation: Support can review incident details and deliver a post incident analysis

options.text: Migrate the workload from Cloud Spanner to a different database to avoid future maintenance
options.explanation: Moving to another database changes operational characteristics and maintenance behavior

answer:
The correct option is Configure a maintenance exclusion window on the Cloud Spanner instance during peak sales hours.

A maintenance exclusion on a Cloud Spanner instance tells Google Cloud to defer planned maintenance during the specified time range. This is the fastest and most targeted way to keep production safe during peak sales windows because it prevents planned updates from starting when you cannot afford any disruption. You can set exclusions that align with concert on sale events so planned maintenance will be delayed until after the window ends.

Upgrade the Cloud Spanner instance to a multi region configuration to avoid maintenance impact is not correct. A multi region configuration improves availability and durability but it does not stop maintenance from occurring. It also is not an immediate mitigation because it requires planning and additional cost.

Open a Support case to investigate why the instance was down for more than 12 minutes is not correct. While it can be useful for root cause analysis it does not immediately prevent maintenance from interrupting future peak events.

Migrate the workload from Cloud Spanner to a different database to avoid future maintenance is not correct. Migration would be complex and slow and every managed database has maintenance. This does not meet the requirement for immediate action.
originalQuery: You manage a healthcare application that uses Cloud Spanner for storing patient data. query: At Nimbus Retail your Cloud SQL for MySQL primary slows down when dashboards trigger heavy read traffic during the late afternoon rush. You need to raise read throughput and lower latency while keeping the production writer unchanged. What should you do?

options.text: Partition frequently read tables in the schema based on time or key access patterns
options.explanation: Table partitioning organizes large tables into smaller partitions that can reduce scanned data and improve query efficiency.

options.text: Enable Cloud SQL high availability for the primary instance
options.explanation: High availability adds a standby instance and automatic failover to increase resiliency of the primary workload.

options.text: Create read replicas and route reporting traffic to them
options.explanation: Read replicas accept read-only queries so they can handle analytics or reporting workloads away from the primary instance.

options.text: Increase the machine type of the primary instance
options.explanation: Upsizing the instance adds more vCPU and memory to the primary database server to provide additional compute resources.

options.text: Move the primary to a larger persistent disk tier with higher IOPS
options.explanation: A faster disk class can provide more IOPS and throughput to the storage layer that serves the primary database.

answer:
The correct options are Partition frequently read tables in the schema based on time or key access patterns and Create read replicas and route reporting traffic to them.

Using read replicas offloads the dashboard queries from the primary so the production writer remains unchanged. Cloud SQL for MySQL supports replicas that handle read only workloads which increases aggregate read throughput and reduces latency when you route reporting traffic to them.

Applying partitioning to the most heavily read tables helps queries scan less data and keep indexes smaller which improves cache efficiency and lowers latency during peak reads. This schema optimization complements replicas and does not change the writer role.

Enable Cloud SQL high availability for the primary instance improves resilience and failover but it does not add read capacity because the standby does not serve traffic in normal operation.

Increase the machine type of the primary instance adds CPU and memory yet all reads still hit a single node which leaves you with the same contention between reads and writes during peak dashboards.

Move the primary to a larger persistent disk tier with higher IOPS can lower storage latency but it does not provide horizontal read scaling and all read traffic still competes on the primary.

query: You administer a Cloud Spanner database for QuickMeal, a food delivery platform. Orders stream into a table named orders_feed in real time, and each record includes a unique orderId and a related zoneId. You must design a reusable parameterized query that is efficient for frequent execution and that retrieves the details for one specific order within a particular zone. What should you do?

options.text: SELECT * FROM orders_feed WHERE order_id=@orderId OR zone_id=@zoneId
options.explanation: This statement returns rows that satisfy either the order identifier or the zone filter which can broaden the result set unintentionally

options.text: SELECT * FROM orders_feed WHERE order_id=@orderId AND zone_id=@zoneId
options.explanation: This statement applies both the order identifier and the zone as parameters to restrict the results to a single targeted order

options.text: SELECT * FROM orders_feed@{FORCE_INDEX=idx_orders_order_id} WHERE order_id=@orderId
options.explanation: This statement forces use of a specific index and filters only by the order identifier which omits the zone filter

options.text: SELECT * FROM orders_feed WHERE order_id=@orderId AND zone_id='APAC'
options.explanation: This statement uses a parameter for the order identifier but hard-codes the zone to APAC which reduces query flexibility

answer:
Only SELECT * FROM orders_feed WHERE order_id=@orderId AND zone_id=@zoneId meets the requirement.

This retrieves the exact order within the specified zone because both predicates must be true for the same row. Using named parameters makes the query reusable and efficient for frequent execution because Cloud Spanner can cache query plans and you avoid hardcoded values. Filtering on both columns also lets the optimizer use a suitable primary key or secondary index if available which reduces the amount of data scanned.

SELECT * FROM orders_feed WHERE order_id=@orderId OR zone_id=@zoneId returns rows that match either the order or the zone which does not guarantee that the order belongs to the given zone. Using OR can also force broader scans and limit the effectiveness of composite indexes.

SELECT * FROM orders_feed@{FORCE_INDEX=idx_orders_order_id} WHERE order_id=@orderId omits the zone filter so it would return the order across all zones which fails the requirement. Forcing an index reduces portability and is unnecessary here because a single column index does not account for the zone filtering requirement.

SELECT * FROM orders_feed WHERE order_id=@orderId AND zone_id='APAC' hardcodes the zone which makes the query not reusable for other zones and does not meet the requirement to parameterize the zone.

query: A retail analytics firm is deploying Bare Metal Solution for Oracle in europe-west1 and the Oracle host must privately reach a Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL instance that resides in us-central1. You already have a Dedicated Interconnect from your on-premises data center to your VPC that is attached in europe-west1. Which networking configuration will allow the Bare Metal Solution system to securely connect to the Cloud SQL instance in us-central1?

options.text: Turn on Private Google Access for the subnets in europe-west1
options.explanation: Private Google Access lets VMs without external IP addresses reach Google APIs and services using private addresses within the subnet

options.text: Build a Cloud VPN tunnel between the Bare Metal Solution environment in europe-west1 and the network segment in us-central1
options.explanation: Cloud VPN provides encrypted connectivity across the internet between two networks or regions

options.text: Set the VPC dynamic routing mode to global so routes from Cloud Router and Cloud Interconnect are usable in all regions
options.explanation: Global dynamic routing mode propagates learned routes across the entire VPC so traffic can reach resources in different regions

options.text: Create a static route on the Bare Metal Solution side that points to the Cloud SQL private IP range in us-central1
options.explanation: A static route manually directs traffic to a specific prefix and does not provide dynamic propagation or automatic failover

answer:
The correct option is Set the VPC dynamic routing mode to global so routes from Cloud Router and Cloud Interconnect are usable in all regions.

With this setting, routes learned over your Dedicated Interconnect by Cloud Router in europe-west1 are distributed to all subnets in the VPC. This makes the private IP range that backs the Cloud SQL instance in us-central1 reachable from the Bare Metal Solution hosts. It also ensures the return path to on premises is available from us-central1 so the connection is symmetric and secure.

Turn on Private Google Access for the subnets in europe-west1 is not relevant because Private Google Access lets VMs without external IPs reach Google APIs and services. It does not influence private IP connectivity to Cloud SQL through your VPC and Interconnect.

Build a Cloud VPN tunnel between the Bare Metal Solution environment in europe-west1 and the network segment in us-central1 is unnecessary and incorrect because you already have Dedicated Interconnect providing private connectivity to the VPC. The issue is route scope across regions and enabling the correct routing mode solves it without adding VPN.

Create a static route on the Bare Metal Solution side that points to the Cloud SQL private IP range in us-central1 will not work because the Cloud SQL private IP network is reached through service networking peering and the VPC relies on Cloud Router to advertise and import routes. A static route on the customer side does not make the route available in other regions and it does not override the peering control of those prefixes.

query: An insurance brokerage plans to move a 28 TB Oracle database from its colocation facility to Google Cloud. They need an approach that keeps cutover downtime very low, permits ongoing schema changes while replication runs, and includes features for data validation and the ability to roll back if needed. They also want to host Oracle on a managed offering in Google Cloud that is built for Oracle workloads. Which combination of Google Cloud migration tooling and managed database service should they choose?

options.text: Cloud Dataflow and Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL
options.explanation: This pairing uses Dataflow to process and load data into a managed PostgreSQL service on Google Cloud.

options.text: Database Migration Service with Bare Metal Solution for Oracle
options.explanation: This approach uses a managed migration service together with a managed bare metal environment that is designed to run Oracle in Google Cloud.

options.text: Datastream and BigQuery
options.explanation: This choice relies on change data capture to stream source changes into BigQuery for analytics workloads.

options.text: Cloud Storage Transfer Service and Cloud Bigtable
options.explanation: This option copies data to Cloud Storage and then stores it in Bigtable which is a wide column NoSQL service.

answer:
The correct choice is Database Migration Service with Bare Metal Solution for Oracle. This pairing delivers continuous replication for very low cutover downtime, supports ongoing schema changes while replication runs, and provides built-in data validation with the ability to revert the cutover plan if needed. Bare Metal Solution gives you a managed environment purpose built for Oracle workloads in Google Cloud.

The migration service continuously replicates changes from the source Oracle database which allows you to keep the target closely synchronized until you are ready to cut over. Because it is designed for Oracle sources it can handle ongoing schema changes during replication so development can continue while the migration proceeds. The service also includes validation features so you can verify data consistency before cutover and you can plan a safe rollback by retaining the source as the system of record until validation is complete.

Bare Metal Solution provides dedicated hardware in Google Cloud that is tuned for Oracle performance and supportability. It is a managed offering that meets Oracle licensing and architectural needs so you can run Oracle databases with predictable performance and enterprise integrations while staying in close proximity to native Google Cloud services.

Cloud Dataflow and Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL is not suitable because Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL is not an Oracle compatible destination and moving a large Oracle database into PostgreSQL requires engine conversion rather than low downtime replication. Dataflow is a data processing service and does not provide the end to end database migration capabilities and rollback controls required here.

Datastream and BigQuery does not fit because BigQuery is an analytics warehouse rather than a transactional database platform for hosting Oracle workloads. While the change data capture service can ingest from Oracle into analytics targets it does not provide a managed Oracle runtime or a straightforward rollback path for a database cutover.

Cloud Storage Transfer Service and Cloud Bigtable is incorrect because the transfer service moves files and objects rather than live database state and Bigtable is a NoSQL wide column store that does not host Oracle databases or support relational features needed by Oracle workloads.

query: At Astra Transit you must right size a Cloud Bigtable deployment for a connected bus telemetry platform. Peak traffic reaches 36,000 writes per second and 24,000 reads per second with 9 TB of stored data. The business requires 99.999% availability and fast read response times. Projections show a 70% increase in both reads per second and writes per second and a 30% increase in storage within the next year. Which instance configuration should you choose to support the expected growth while keeping costs efficient?

options.text: 15 node regional instance with HDD storage
options.explanation: This config uses a single region with HDD disks and 15 nodes which favors throughput but has higher read latency.

options.text: Two region instance with multi cluster replication and 12 nodes per cluster on SSD
options.explanation: This sets up a Bigtable instance with two clusters in different regions using SSDs and 12 nodes in each cluster.

options.text: 20 node regional instance with SSD storage
options.explanation: This is a single regional cluster that uses SSDs with 20 nodes sized for higher QPS.

options.text: Two region instance with multi cluster replication and 10 nodes per cluster on HDD
options.explanation: This deploys two clusters in separate regions using HDD disks with 10 nodes each.

answer:
The correct option is Two region instance with multi cluster replication and 12 nodes per cluster on SSD.

The business requirement of 99.999% availability points directly to multi cluster replication across two regions because this configuration is designed for very high availability and resilient failover. Using SSD meets the need for fast read response times since SSD provides lower latency and higher random read performance than HDD. With this design you can route traffic across clusters and continue serving if a region becomes unavailable.

Traffic is projected to grow to about 61,000 writes per second and 41,000 reads per second along with a storage increase from 9 TB to roughly 12 TB. Each region should be able to handle the full peak during a failover which means sizing per cluster for the entire expected workload rather than only half. Twelve nodes per cluster on SSD provides ample headroom for these read and write rates and for compactions and bursts while also comfortably covering the storage growth within recommended per node limits. This balances performance and cost and avoids overprovisioning while still meeting the stringent availability target.

15 node regional instance with HDD storage is not suitable because it lacks multi cluster replication and cannot meet a five nines availability target. HDD also delivers higher latency and lower random read performance which conflicts with the fast read requirement.

20 node regional instance with SSD storage offers solid performance but it is still a single region deployment and therefore does not meet the 99.999% availability requirement.

Two region instance with multi cluster replication and 10 nodes per cluster on HDD does include replication across regions but HDD undermines fast read latency and lowers per node throughput for random workloads. Ten nodes per cluster would also be tight during a regional failover when one cluster must absorb the entire peak load and growth.

query: At scrumtuous.com you oversee databases on Google Cloud and leadership wants lower costs and faster queries while maintaining reliability. Which approaches would most effectively improve both cost and performance?

options.text: Move every workload to Cloud Bigtable to gain high throughput characteristics
options.explanation: Cloud Bigtable is a wide column NoSQL service that offers very high throughput for specific access patterns and large scale datasets

options.text: Implement a caching layer with Cloud Memorystore for hot data
options.explanation: This adds an in memory cache that serves frequently accessed keys which can reduce pressure on the primary database and lower latency

options.text: Enable compute autoscaling for Cloud SQL instances to absorb traffic surges
options.explanation: Autoscaling can adjust CPU and memory for Cloud SQL instances to better match demand during peak periods

options.text: Use Cloud SQL with automated backups and binary logging disabled
options.explanation: Disabling backups and binary logging removes operational overhead but eliminates point in time recovery and increases risk

options.text: Adopt a data design that uses partitioning sharding and well tuned indexing
options.explanation: Partitioning sharding and indexing distribute workload and improve query efficiency which can cut costs and reduce response times

answer:
The correct options are Implement a caching layer with Cloud Memorystore for hot data and Adopt a data design that uses partitioning sharding and well tuned indexing.

The first choice offloads frequent reads from the primary databases to an in memory store, which cuts latency and reduces database CPU and IOPS. With fewer expensive reads hitting the backend you can often use smaller instance sizes or fewer replicas which lowers cost while maintaining reliability through a managed service that supports high availability.

The second choice improves how data is organized and accessed. Splitting large datasets by time or key range reduces the amount of data scanned per query and distributing data across shards removes hotspots. Well considered indexes let the engine find rows quickly which shortens execution time and reduces resource consumption. These practices improve performance and can reduce spend without compromising durability or availability.

Move every workload to Cloud Bigtable to gain high throughput characteristics is not appropriate for all database workloads. Bigtable is excellent for very large scale wide column and time series access patterns but it does not provide relational features such as joins and multi row transactions. For typical transactional workloads this migration can increase complexity and cost rather than improve both objectives.

Enable compute autoscaling for Cloud SQL instances to absorb traffic surges is incorrect because Cloud SQL does not automatically scale CPU and memory for a single instance. You must change machine shapes or add read replicas, and storage can autoscale but compute does not, so this choice would not deliver the promised benefit.

Use Cloud SQL with automated backups and binary logging disabled undermines reliability. Disabling backups and binlog removes point in time recovery and complicates replication, which risks data loss. Any small cost savings would come at the expense of the reliability requirement.
originalQuery: In a Google Cloud environment, you are tasked with optimizing both the cost and performance of a database. You have been asked to choose two strategies that would be most effective in achieving this goal. Which of the following options should you select? (Choose two)
originalOptions:

tip: When a question ties together lower cost, faster queries and reliability, favor options that reduce load such as caching or strong data modeling and avoid choices that disable protection features or claim capabilities that the service does not provide.

query: A subscription commerce team at example.com needs a highly available PostgreSQL deployment on Google Cloud. The database must continue to serve requests if one zone in us-east4 becomes unavailable, and all consuming applications run in the same region. Which architecture should you implement?

options.text: Deploy a multi regional GKE cluster and run PostgreSQL with a StatefulSet that uses PersistentVolumeClaims
options.explanation: This approach runs PostgreSQL on Kubernetes and relies on persistent volumes managed by a StatefulSet across a Kubernetes cluster that spans multiple locations

options.text: Run the PostgreSQL servers in one zone and store data on zonal persistent disks
options.explanation: This places both compute and storage in a single failure domain which concentrates risk in one zone

options.text: Create a regional stateful managed instance group for PostgreSQL and use regional persistent disks for the data volume
options.explanation: This design distributes instances across zones within a region and uses synchronously replicated disks that can be reattached in another zone during a zonal outage

options.text: Use a managed instance group with autoscaling and autohealing across multiple zones
options.explanation: This relies on health checks and scaling behavior of a managed instance group that places instances in more than one zone

answer:
The correct answer is Create a regional stateful managed instance group for PostgreSQL and use regional persistent disks for the data volume.

This design places identical database instances across multiple zones in the us-east4 region and preserves each instance’s data with a stateful configuration. The storage layer replicates writes synchronously to another zone so the database can fail over to a healthy zone without data loss. The group distributes virtual machines across zones and when a zone fails it can recreate the instance in a surviving zone while reattaching the replicated volume so the service continues to serve requests for applications in the same region.

Deploy a multi regional GKE cluster and run PostgreSQL with a StatefulSet that uses PersistentVolumeClaims is not appropriate because GKE does not offer a single multi regional cluster and StatefulSets typically bind volumes to a specific zone unless you design for regional volumes. The requirement is to remain within one region and survive a zone outage which is met more directly with a regional compute design and regionally replicated storage.

Run the PostgreSQL servers in one zone and store data on zonal persistent disks would fail if that zone becomes unavailable because both the instances and the data are tied to a single zone and cannot continue serving.

Use a managed instance group with autoscaling and autohealing across multiple zones addresses instance availability but not data durability. Without a stateful configuration and storage that replicates across zones the group may recreate or move instances without their data which risks downtime or data loss for a database workload. Autoscaling is also not a good fit for a stateful relational database.
originalQuery: You are deploying a highly available PostgreSQL database on Google Cloud and you want to ensure that the database remains available even if a single zone goes down. The database will be accessed by services running in the same region. Which configuration should you choose?

tip: When a requirement says the database must survive a zone outage in one region, look for regional resources and a stateful design. Pair compute spread across zones with storage that replicates synchronously across zones.

query: A gaming analytics team at scrumtuous.com is building a near real time metrics service on Google Cloud that must handle very low latency writes for a heavy event stream. The current rate is about 60,000 events per second and you expect it to grow to roughly 180,000 events per second within the next 18 months. You need a managed database that supports this load today and can scale smoothly as traffic increases while keeping latency low. Which solution should you choose?

options.text: BigQuery with streaming inserts into partitioned tables and BI Engine
options.explanation: This approach ingests data into BigQuery for analytical queries by continuously streaming rows into time partitioned tables.

options.text: Cloud Spanner with a multi region instance and scale nodes as needed with hotspot aware key design
options.explanation: Cloud Spanner provides horizontally scalable relational storage with strong consistency and can add nodes to increase throughput.

options.text: Cloud Bigtable with autoscaling enabled and three clusters for multi cluster replication
options.explanation: Cloud Bigtable is a wide column database that supports very high write throughput and can scale automatically across multiple clusters.

options.text: Cloud SQL with read replicas and upgrade the primary instance size when demand grows
options.explanation: Cloud SQL provides managed relational databases that scale primarily by increasing machine size and adding replicas for read traffic.

answer:
The correct option is Cloud Bigtable with autoscaling enabled and three clusters for multi cluster replication.

Bigtable is purpose built for extremely high write throughput with very low latency for single row operations. It scales horizontally by adding nodes and can handle sustained event streams at the scale in the question while keeping latency in the single digit millisecond range. Autoscaling adjusts cluster size based on workload which reduces manual capacity planning as traffic grows from sixty thousand to one hundred eighty thousand events per second.

With three clusters using multi cluster replication, Bigtable improves availability and can use multi cluster routing to distribute requests to healthy clusters. This supports smooth scaling under heavy ingestion and provides resilience during regional issues while keeping write latency low for near real time metrics.

BigQuery with streaming inserts into partitioned tables and BI Engine is designed for analytics rather than as a low latency operational store. Streaming inserts have quotas and can introduce variability in availability for querying, and BI Engine accelerates query performance rather than ingestion. This does not meet very low latency write requirements at this scale.

Cloud Spanner with a multi region instance and scale nodes as needed with hotspot aware key design can scale, yet multi region configurations require cross region quorum which increases write latency. The workload does not need relational transactions or strong SQL semantics, so the added latency and cost are not justified compared to a wide column store optimized for high write throughput.

Cloud SQL with read replicas and upgrade the primary instance size when demand grows cannot meet the sustained write rate because there is a single primary for writes and read replicas only help reads. Vertical scaling of the primary will hit limits long before reaching the required throughput and latency targets.
originalQuery: Your company is developing a real-time analytics application on Google Cloud Platform (GCP) that requires low-latency processing of a high volume of streaming data. The current workload is 50,000 events per second (EPS), and you expect this to increase to 150,000 EPS over the next two years. tip: Match the workload to the storage model. For sustained write heavy ingestion with low latency and linear horizontal scaling, favor Cloud Bigtable. If you see strong consistency across regions or SQL transactions as primary needs, then consider Cloud Spanner instead.

query: A retail startup at mcnz.com operates its primary order processing system on Cloud Spanner in one region. You need to design disaster recovery for a potential regional outage while meeting a very small recovery point objective and a rapid recovery time objective. Which actions should you implement?

options.text: Maintain a cold standby Spanner instance in a separate region
options.explanation: A cold standby remains inactive until a disruption occurs and would require data restoration and promotion steps before serving production traffic

options.text: Migrate the database to a Cloud Spanner multi region configuration
options.explanation: A multi region configuration replicates data across regions using synchronous replication and supports automatic failover during a regional disruption

options.text: Consolidate the deployment into a single region to simplify operations
options.explanation: A single region instance can reduce cost and management overhead but concentrates availability risk in one location

options.text: Schedule automated backups of the Spanner database to Cloud Storage
options.explanation: Automated backups create restorable point in time copies stored in Cloud Storage to recover from accidental deletion or corruption

options.text: Enable automatic database tuning features
options.explanation: Automatic tuning focuses on performance adjustments such as query plans or resource settings rather than cross region availability

answer:
The correct actions are Migrate the database to a Cloud Spanner multi region configuration and Schedule automated backups of the Spanner database to Cloud Storage.

A multi region Spanner deployment provides synchronous replication across regions with automatic failover, which delivers a very small recovery point objective and a rapid recovery time objective for a regional outage. Writes commit only after achieving quorum across replicas, so data loss is minimized, and failover is handled by the service which keeps recovery fast and predictable.

Regularly scheduled backups add a second layer of protection by enabling recovery from data corruption or accidental deletion. Keeping backups in an independent storage location and automating their creation ensures you can restore to a known good state while the multi region design handles live regional outages with minimal disruption.

Maintain a cold standby Spanner instance in a separate region is insufficient because Spanner does not support ad hoc cross instance replication, and a cold standby would require manual promotion and data synchronization which increases both RPO and RTO.

Consolidate the deployment into a single region to simplify operations reduces resilience and directly contradicts the requirement to withstand a regional outage while maintaining very small RPO and rapid RTO.

Enable automatic database tuning features may improve performance or efficiency, yet it does not provide the cross regional redundancy or restore capabilities needed to meet the disaster recovery objectives.

query: You manage a high-traffic payment ledger for a regional retailer that stores its data in Cloud Spanner. A scheduled release includes a schema change and your business can tolerate less than 7 minutes of service interruption. How should you carry out the schema update to meet this requirement?

options.text: Use Cloud Spanner backups to take a snapshot before the release, apply the schema change, and rely on restore if issues occur
options.explanation: This choice creates a safety net by taking a backup before making schema modifications and depends on restore for rollback

options.text: Migrate the workload to Cloud SQL to modify the schema, then move the data back to Cloud Spanner
options.explanation: This choice moves data to a different managed database to perform the change and later brings it back

options.text: Run the DDL directly on Cloud Spanner because it supports online schema changes without taking the database offline
options.explanation: This approach applies schema DDL on a live Spanner database and relies on its online schema update capability

options.text: Set up Cloud Spanner change streams and a Dataflow pipeline to sync to another Spanner database, update the schema on the copy, then cut over the application
options.explanation: This approach builds a replication pipeline to another Spanner database for a cutover after the schema is modified on the copy

answer:
The correct option is Run the DDL directly on Cloud Spanner because it supports online schema changes without taking the database offline.

This approach meets the requirement because Cloud Spanner performs most schema updates online. Operations such as adding columns or creating indexes run as long running background tasks while the database remains available to serve traffic. You can apply the change and monitor the progress without taking an outage, which comfortably fits a tolerance of less than seven minutes of disruption.

Use Cloud Spanner backups to take a snapshot before the release, apply the schema change, and rely on restore if issues occur is not appropriate because restores create a new database and take significant time. A rollback through restore would far exceed the allowed interruption and would require complex cutover steps.

Migrate the workload to Cloud SQL to modify the schema, then move the data back to Cloud Spanner is incorrect because moving between these different database platforms is complex and time consuming. It introduces far more risk and downtime than necessary and does not leverage the native online schema capabilities of Spanner.

Set up Cloud Spanner change streams and a Dataflow pipeline to sync to another Spanner database, update the schema on the copy, then cut over the application is unnecessary and adds heavy operational complexity. This pattern is for change data capture and replication rather than online schema management, and the cutover could easily exceed the downtime budget.
originalQuery: You are in charge of a critical application that uses Cloud Spanner as its primary data store. There's an upcoming maintenance window during which you need to upgrade your schema. The application cannot afford more than 10 minutes of downtime. Which method should you employ to achieve this?
originalOptions:
A. Apply schema updates directly as Cloud Spanner supports online schema updates without downtime.
B. Conduct a hot backup of Cloud Spanner, perform the schema update, and restore the backup if needed.
C. Use the Cloud Spanner Dataflow connector to replicate data, update the schema on the replica, and then switch traffic.
D. Migrate data to a Cloud SQL instance, perform schema update, and migrate back to Cloud Spanner.
domain: Deploy scalable and highly available databases in Google Cloud
tip: When a service explicitly supports online schema changes, prefer the native DDL path. Be wary of answers that add migrations, restores, or complex replication topologies because those usually increase downtime and risk without benefit.

query: Orion Payments operates a production Cloud SQL for MySQL 5.7 instance in us-central1 and must move to MySQL 8.0 while keeping the application outage under 3 minutes and preserving transactional integrity throughout the upgrade. What approach should be taken to meet these requirements?

options.text: Create a Cloud SQL read replica of the MySQL 5.7 instance and promote the replica during a maintenance window to minimize downtime
options.explanation: This option attempts to reduce downtime by promoting a synchronized replica to primary after replication catches up

options.text: Provision a new Cloud SQL for MySQL 8.0 instance, run Database Migration Service in continuous mode to replicate from the 5.7 source, then perform a brief cutover
options.explanation: This option sets up a new target on the desired version and continuously replicates changes until a short switchover is performed

options.text: Export a logical dump from the MySQL 5.7 instance, create a new MySQL 8.0 instance, import the dump, and point the application to the new endpoint
options.explanation: This option migrates data using an offline export and import process before redirecting application traffic

options.text: Migrate the workload to Cloud Spanner and decommission the Cloud SQL instance after the data is moved
options.explanation: This option replaces the current database engine with a different managed service and requires a platform migration

answer:
The correct option is Provision a new Cloud SQL for MySQL 8.0 instance, run Database Migration Service in continuous mode to replicate from the 5.7 source, then perform a brief cutover.

Using DMS in continuous mode performs an initial load and then streams ongoing changes from the MySQL 5.7 source using binary logs so the MySQL 8.0 destination stays nearly caught up. At cutover you pause writes on the source, wait for replication to reach zero lag, and then update the application to point to the new Cloud SQL instance. This approach routinely achieves a few minutes of downtime and preserves transactional integrity because changes are replayed in order.

Create a Cloud SQL read replica of the MySQL 5.7 instance and promote the replica during a maintenance window to minimize downtime is incorrect because a read replica shares the same major version as its primary. Promotion does not change the version, so you would still be on MySQL 5.7 and you would not meet the requirement to upgrade to 8.0.

Export a logical dump from the MySQL 5.7 instance, create a new MySQL 8.0 instance, import the dump, and point the application to the new endpoint is incorrect because a dump and restore requires either a lengthy write freeze or additional tooling to capture changes during the import. This makes it difficult to hold downtime under three minutes and risks transactional gaps unless writes are fully stopped for the entire duration.

Migrate the workload to Cloud Spanner and decommission the Cloud SQL instance after the data is moved is incorrect because this changes the database engine and typically requires application and schema changes. It does not satisfy the requirement to upgrade the existing MySQL deployment to version 8.0.
originalQuery: A Database Engineer is tasked with planning an upgrade for a Google Cloud-managed database. The current setup consists of a Cloud SQL instance running MySQL 5.7. The engineer needs to upgrade the instance to MySQL 8.0 with minimal downtime while ensuring data consistency. Which of the following approaches is the best option to achieve this goal?
originalOptions:
A. Use Cloud Spanner instead of Cloud SQL to upgrade the database and then migrate the data.
B. Perform a rolling update on the Cloud SQL instance to upgrade it from MySQL 5.7 to 8.0.
C. Export the data from the Cloud SQL instance, create a new Cloud SQL instance with MySQL 8.0, import the data, and then switch the application to use the new instance.
D. Create a new Cloud SQL instance running MySQL 8.0, use Cloud SQL Data Migration Service to migrate the data, and then switch the application to use the new instance.
domain: Migrate data solutions
tip: When a scenario requires minimal downtime and transactional integrity during a version upgrade, look for continuous replication with a planned cutover rather than one time exports or replica promotion.

query: An analytics team at scrumtuous.com stores high volume telemetry in Cloud Bigtable. Most dashboards query the most recent 21 days and must return in milliseconds, while data older than 270 days is retained mostly for compliance and is rarely read. You want to keep costs in check without hurting interactive performance for the user facing workload. Which storage choice in Bigtable should you use for the instance that serves these queries?

options.text: Configure HDD storage for the primary cluster that handles live user reads
options.explanation: HDD storage reduces cost per gigabyte but provides lower throughput and higher latency compared to SSD for interactive workloads.

options.text: Deploy Bigtable with cross region replication to multiple regions for faster reads
options.explanation: Cross region replication can improve availability and locality for reads but it does not change the storage media characteristics.

options.text: Use SSD storage for the Bigtable cluster that powers dashboard queries
options.explanation: SSD storage delivers high throughput and low latency which suits frequent reads and writes to recent time series data.

options.text: Enable automatic tiering between SSD and HDD within one Bigtable instance
options.explanation: Storage tiering within a single Bigtable instance would mix media types to balance cost and performance for the same table.

answer:
The correct option is Use SSD storage for the Bigtable cluster that powers dashboard queries. The other choices either reduce performance, increase cost without benefit, or are not supported.

Interactive dashboards that must return in milliseconds rely on low latency random reads, and this storage type is recommended by Google Cloud for production user facing workloads. It provides the throughput and tail latency characteristics needed for the hot 21 day working set. Retaining older data for compliance does not change the requirement for fast access to recent data, and you can keep costs in control by right sizing nodes and using garbage collection policies rather than selecting a slower medium.

Configure HDD storage for the primary cluster that handles live user reads is not appropriate because that medium is optimized for large sequential scans and has significantly higher read latency. It would harm the interactive experience for dashboard users.

Deploy Bigtable with cross region replication to multiple regions for faster reads does not address the latency requirement for a single region dashboard and it adds substantial cost and operational overhead. Replication is primarily for availability and disaster recovery and it can also add write latency.

Enable automatic tiering between SSD and HDD within one Bigtable instance is not possible in Bigtable. The storage type is chosen at cluster creation and you cannot mix or automatically tier storage types within the same instance.
originalQuery: Your application uses Google Cloud Bigtable for storing large amounts of time-series data. To optimize performance and cost, you need to choose the appropriate storage option. Which of the following would you select to meet these requirements?
originalOptions:
A. Implement a multi-regional Bigtable instance to provide redundancy and low-latency access.
B. Use SSD storage in Bigtable for high throughput and low latency access to recent data.
C. Set up automatic data archiving for Bigtable to move older data to Cloud Storage for cost savings.
D. Opt for HDD storage in Bigtable for less frequently accessed, historical time-series data.
domain: Design scalable and highly available cloud database solutions
tip: Match the workload to the storage type. Choose SSD when you see latency sensitive random reads and avoid options that add cost without a clear performance benefit or that describe a feature that does not exist.

query: At Crestline Media you must right size a new Cloud SQL instance using observed performance and planned growth. Current peaks average 4200 queries per second, 2.5 TB of data, 8000 simultaneous connections and 200 GB of backup usage. The business projects a 60% rise in traffic and a 25% increase in stored data within the next 12 months. Which instance configuration will support the forecast while keeping costs efficient?

options.text: db-n2-standard-32 with 6 TB of HDD storage
options.explanation: This uses a standard memory machine type with 32 vCPUs and lower cost HDD persistent disks that prioritize capacity over performance

options.text: db-n2-highmem-32 with 4 TB of SSD storage
options.explanation: This uses a high memory 32 vCPU machine with SSD persistent disks sized to cover the expected data volume and provide strong IOPS

options.text: db-n2-highmem-64 with 6 TB of SSD storage
options.explanation: This provides a high memory 64 vCPU machine and larger SSD capacity that offers substantial headroom for compute and storage

options.text: db-n2-highmem-16 with 3 TB of SSD storage
options.explanation: This is a high memory 16 vCPU machine with SSD storage that favors lower cost but with reduced compute and capacity

answer:
The correct choice is db-n2-highmem-32 with 4 TB of SSD storage because it meets the projected workload while staying cost efficient.

Current peaks of 4200 queries per second and 2.5 TB of data are expected to grow to roughly 6700 queries per second and about 3.1 TB of data over the next year. A 4 TB SSD allocation provides enough capacity for the data growth plus room for indexes, temporary space, and maintenance operations. SSD is recommended for high throughput transactional workloads because it delivers the IOPS and latency needed for sustained query rates and predictable performance. Storage auto increase can be enabled to provide headroom without overcommitting on day one.

The n2 high-memory profile at 32 vCPUs gives a strong balance of compute and RAM so caches and buffers can serve more reads and the instance can tolerate large numbers of connections. If connection surges occur you can use connection pooling to manage client concurrency while keeping instance resources efficient. This configuration therefore aligns with the performance target and cost control goals.

db-n2-standard-32 with 6 TB of HDD storage is not appropriate for high query rates because HDD throughput and IOPS are significantly lower than SSD which leads to latency under load. It also allocates less memory per vCPU than a high-memory profile which reduces cache effectiveness.

db-n2-highmem-64 with 6 TB of SSD storage would handle the workload but it is overprovisioned for the forecast and increases cost unnecessarily. You can meet the targets with the smaller high-memory node and still enable storage auto increase for growth.

db-n2-highmem-16 with 3 TB of SSD storage is likely to be constrained on CPU and memory at the forecasted query rate and the storage size leaves too little buffer over the expected 3.1 TB which risks running short once overhead is considered.
originalQuery: A Database Engineer has been tasked with sizing a Cloud SQL instance based on the current environment workload metrics and future requirements. The current average workload metrics are as follows: 5000 queries per second during peak times 3 TB of data storage 10,000 concurrent connections 150 GB of backup storage The company is expecting a 50% increase in workload and a 20% increase in data storage over the next year. Which of the following instance configurations is the most appropriate to handle the anticipated growth while minimizing costs?
originalOptions:
A. db-n1-highmem-16 with 4 TB of SSD storage
B. db-n1-highmem-64 with 6 TB of SSD storage
C. db-n1-highmem-32 with 4 TB of SSD storage
D. db-n1-standard-32 with 6 TB of HDD storage
domain: Deploy scalable and highly available databases in Google Cloud
tip: Estimate growth first and translate it into compute, memory, and storage needs. Prefer SSD for high QPS and leave headroom for indexes and temporary space. Use connection pooling to control concurrency before jumping to a larger machine.

query: A small online learning startup named StudyWell has operated a production Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL instance for nine months and Cloud Monitoring shows CPU usage stays under 12 percent and memory usage remains below 35 percent for most of the day. You want to lower monthly spend without harming performance during busy periods. What should you do?

options.text: Use Cloud SQL Insights to analyze slow queries and tune performance
options.explanation: This tool helps you visualize query performance and locate slow statements.

options.text: Follow the guidance from the Cloud SQL overprovisioned recommender
options.explanation: This recommender suggests downsizing instance resources when utilization is consistently low.

options.text: Reduce the disk capacity of the instance to a smaller size
options.explanation: This action attempts to reduce provisioned storage to lower storage charges.

options.text: Enable high availability for the instance to improve reliability
options.explanation: This feature creates a standby in another zone to provide automatic failover.

answer:
The correct option is Follow the guidance from the Cloud SQL overprovisioned recommender.

This guidance is designed to identify instances that consistently run below their capacity and it recommends a smaller machine type or fewer vCPUs and memory while maintaining headroom for peak load. Your instance has shown many months of low CPU and memory usage which strongly indicates overprovisioning. Acting on these recommendations lowers compute costs while protecting performance during busier periods because the analysis uses sustained utilization and safe thresholds.

Use Cloud SQL Insights to analyze slow queries and tune performance is not the best action when the goal is to reduce instance cost from low utilization. Insights helps find and fix query issues but it does not rightsize the instance or directly reduce spend.

Reduce the disk capacity of the instance to a smaller size is not feasible because Cloud SQL storage can be increased but cannot be decreased. Shrinking storage would not address compute overprovisioning anyway.

Enable high availability for the instance to improve reliability would add redundancy and improve uptime but it increases cost rather than lowering it, so it does not meet the objective.
originalQuery: You have been running a PostgreSQL instance on Cloud SQL in Google Cloud for a year. Monitoring indicates low CPU utilization and memory usage for extended periods. You need to reduce costs without impacting performance. What should you do?
originalOptions:
A. Enable high availability for the instance to automatically reduce unused resources.
B. Scale down the disk size to reduce costs, as the utilization is low.
C. Use Cloud SQL Insights to analyze resource-intensive queries and identify cost-saving opportunities.
D. Apply the recommendations from the Cloud SQL overprovisioned recommender.
domain: Deploy scalable and highly available databases in Google Cloud
tip: When utilization is consistently low for months, think of rightsizing with the appropriate recommender. Remember that you cannot decrease storage on Cloud SQL and that high availability improves reliability but increases cost.

query: Skylark Outfitters runs its checkout and inventory on Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL. They need to add keyword product search across about 250,000 SKUs, and the new search must not impact the performance of the transactional database. What should they implement?

options.text: Export transactional data to BigQuery on a schedule and run keyword searches in BigQuery
options.explanation: This approach moves data into an analytics warehouse for querying but is typically batch oriented and not tuned for low latency full text search.

options.text: Integrate Cloud SQL with a managed search platform such as Elasticsearch or OpenSearch and run searches there
options.explanation: A dedicated search engine provides inverted indexes and relevance ranking and it can be fed continuously from the source database using connectors or pipelines.

options.text: Enable full text search in Cloud SQL and issue all keyword queries on the transactional instance
options.explanation: Running search on the same instance shares CPU and memory with OLTP workload and can contend with transactional performance.

options.text: Create a Cloud SQL read replica and route keyword searches to the replica
options.explanation: A read replica can offload reads yet it still uses the database engine and lacks the specialized indexing and scoring used by dedicated search systems.

answer:
The correct choice is Integrate Cloud SQL with a managed search platform such as Elasticsearch or OpenSearch and run searches there.

This approach offloads indexing and query load to a system designed for full text search. Search engines provide inverted indexes, relevance scoring, stemming, synonyms, and horizontal scalability that handle 250,000 SKUs with low latency. Cloud SQL remains focused on transactional workloads so you avoid contention on CPU, memory, and IOPS. You can synchronize data through change data capture or batch pipelines so the search index stays current without burdening the database.

Export transactional data to BigQuery on a schedule and run keyword searches in BigQuery is not suitable for user facing search because BigQuery is optimized for analytical workloads and not for low latency interactive keyword queries. Scheduled exports introduce staleness which undermines inventory accuracy during checkout.

Enable full text search in Cloud SQL and issue all keyword queries on the transactional instance violates the requirement to avoid performance impact. Even with GIN or GIST indexes and PostgreSQL full text features, heavy search traffic competes with OLTP workload and index maintenance increases write overhead.

Create a Cloud SQL read replica and route keyword searches to the replica reduces pressure on the primary but it still requires maintaining full text indexes and can cause replication lag under heavy search load. It also lacks the advanced search relevance and scalability of a dedicated search engine and there is still operational coupling to the database tier.
originalQuery: Your company is using a Cloud SQL database to handle e-commerce transactions. You want to add a search feature that enables customers to search for products by keyword. This feature should not impact the performance of the transactional database. What should you do?
originalOptions:
A. Use a separate Cloud Spanner instance for handling search queries. Sync the data from Cloud SQL to Cloud Spanner.
B. Enable Cloud SQL full-text search capabilities and perform all search queries directly on the transactional database.
C. Integrate the transactional database with a managed search service such as Elasticsearch or OpenSearch. Perform search queries on this service.
D. Use BigQuery to import the transactional data and run keyword searches on BigQuery.
domain: Manage a solution that can span multiple database solutions
tip: When a question says the new feature must not impact the transactional database and it involves keyword search or relevance ranking, prefer an external search engine that is built for that purpose and keep OLTP on Cloud SQL.

query: You oversee a logistics tracking platform at NorthPeak Shipping that uses Cloud Firestore in Native mode. Regulators require a complete archive of every document create update and delete for long term retention and the application must keep read and write latency as low as possible even with approximately 300000 writes per day. Which approach should you implement to satisfy these requirements?

options.text: Build a custom change data capture pipeline with Cloud Pub/Sub that publishes an event from the application before each write to Firestore
options.explanation: This relies on application code to publish messages that represent mutations which can then be stored as an audit log.

options.text: Enable Firestore managed export to Cloud Storage on a recurring schedule to keep copies of collections
options.explanation: This performs snapshot style exports of Firestore data to Cloud Storage on demand or via a schedule rather than capturing every individual change.

options.text: Use Cloud Functions for Firestore document triggers to record each create update and delete to an immutable archive
options.explanation: This approach uses Firestore event driven triggers that emit a record for each document change which can be written to Cloud Storage or BigQuery.

options.text: Database Migration Service
options.explanation: This service handles migrations and replication for relational databases into Cloud SQL and does not integrate with Cloud Firestore.

answer:
The correct option is Use Cloud Functions for Firestore document triggers to record each create update and delete to an immutable archive.

This approach listens to actual database events so it captures creates updates and deletes after they are committed which ensures a complete and reliable audit trail. It runs asynchronously from the client write path so application reads and writes remain low latency even as volume grows to hundreds of thousands of writes per day. You can write each change to an append only target with retention controls to meet long term archival requirements and you can design the handler to be idempotent for reliability and scale.

Build a custom change data capture pipeline with Cloud Pub/Sub that publishes an event from the application before each write to Firestore is not reliable for regulatory archiving because it records intent rather than confirmed database changes and it can drift from the source of truth if a write fails or if a path bypasses the publisher. It also adds work to the application path and does not inherently provide an immutable archive.

Enable Firestore managed export to Cloud Storage on a recurring schedule to keep copies of collections produces periodic snapshots rather than a stream of every change. This misses individual mutations between exports and cannot guarantee a complete per operation history which makes it unsuitable for strict auditing while also offering no latency benefit to the application.

Database Migration Service is for moving data between supported databases and is not a mechanism for recording Firestore change events or building a long term audit log.
originalQuery: You're managing a high-throughput application that uses Cloud Firestore in Native mode. Due to regulatory compliance, you need to archive all document changes while ensuring minimal latency in document reads and writes. Which method should you employ?
originalOptions:
A. Deploy a parallel Firestore in Datastore mode and replicate changes.
B. Enable Firestore's managed export to Cloud Storage.
C. Implement Firestore triggers with Cloud Functions to capture changes and archive them.
D. Use Cloud Pub/Sub to create a change data capture (CDC) system.
domain: Design scalable and highly available cloud database solutions
tip: When you see requirements for every change and low latency think event driven triggers on the data store rather than scheduled exports or app originated events. Prefer asynchronous server side capture that fires on committed writes.

query: A compliance lead at mcnz.com needs disaster recovery for a Cloud SQL for MySQL database that runs in us-central1. The dataset is highly sensitive so the replication must protect integrity and use encryption while it copies to a standby instance in europe-west4. What should you implement to meet these requirements?

options.text: Use Pub/Sub with Cloud Functions to write changes to a second database
options.explanation: This approach streams messages and has functions insert records into another database but it does not provide database level replication features

options.text: Configure Cloud SQL native replication and use CMEK
options.explanation: This sets up a Cloud SQL replica in another region using the built in replication capability while using a customer managed key for encryption at rest

options.text: Enable CMEK on the primary Cloud SQL for MySQL instance
options.explanation: This applies customer managed encryption to the storage of the source database but it does not establish any replica

options.text: Datastream
options.explanation: This service captures changes from MySQL and streams them to targets like BigQuery or Cloud Storage rather than creating a Cloud SQL replica

answer:
The correct option is Configure Cloud SQL native replication and use CMEK.

Cloud SQL for MySQL supports cross region read replicas that you can place in europe-west4 while the primary remains in us-central1. This native replication keeps data integrity through managed MySQL replication and the service encrypts data in transit. Using customer managed encryption keys ensures that data at rest and backups are encrypted with your own keys in both regions. You create the replica in europe-west4 and supply a key in that region so the standby remains encrypted under your control. This approach gives you a straightforward path to disaster recovery because you can promote the replica if the primary region is unavailable.

Use Pub/Sub with Cloud Functions to write changes to a second database is not a supported or reliable mechanism for MySQL replication. It does not provide ordered transactional consistency and it cannot act as a managed standby for Cloud SQL, which risks data loss and integrity issues.

Enable CMEK on the primary Cloud SQL for MySQL instance does not meet the disaster recovery requirement because it does not create a standby in europe-west4. In addition, CMEK must be configured when an instance is created, so you cannot simply turn it on later for an existing primary, and enabling it on the primary alone would not set up replication.

Datastream is a change data capture service that is commonly used for migrations or analytics pipelines. It does not create a managed MySQL standby in Cloud SQL and it does not provide the simple promotion and failover workflow you need for disaster recovery.
originalQuery: You have been tasked with replicating data from a Cloud SQL for MySQL instance to a secondary location for disaster recovery purposes. The data in the primary instance is sensitive, and you need to ensure data integrity and encryption during the replication process. Which of the following options should you select?
originalOptions:
A. Set up Cloud SQL for MySQL with Customer-Managed Encryption Keys (CMEK).
B. Use Cloud SQL's built-in replication with CMEK.
C. Use Pub/Sub with a Cloud Function to insert data into a secondary database.
D. Use BigQuery Data Transfer Service.
domain: Deploy scalable and highly available databases in Google Cloud
tip: When you see cross region disaster recovery for Cloud SQL, look for native read replicas and think about promotion during a regional outage. If the question stresses sensitive data, pair the replica with CMEK and remember CMEK must be chosen at instance creation.

query: Riverpine Labs has just deployed a Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL instance and is connecting from a Compute Engine VM using the Cloud SQL Auth Proxy. The proxy logs show Error 404 Not Found whenever a connection attempt is made. What should you do first to fix the issue?

options.text: Enable the Cloud SQL Admin API in the Google Cloud project
options.explanation: This action allows the proxy to call the service that provides instance metadata and connection information

options.text: Verify that the proxy is targeting the correct Google Cloud project in its configuration
options.explanation: If the proxy points to the wrong project then it may not find the intended instance by name

options.text: Double check that the instance connection name in the proxy flags exactly matches the project region and instance ID
options.explanation: The proxy resolves the endpoint based on the full connection name which includes the project ID the region and the instance name

options.text: Grant the service account the Cloud SQL Client role
options.explanation: This role provides permissions required for the service account to initiate authorized connections to Cloud SQL

answer:
The correct option is Double check that the instance connection name in the proxy flags exactly matches the project region and instance ID.

A 404 Not Found from the Cloud SQL Auth Proxy means the resource the proxy requested does not exist under the identifier it used. The proxy identifies your instance through the instance connection name which must match the project the region and the instance ID exactly and must use the format with the three parts separated by colons. Any typo such as a wrong project or region or instance ID will cause the proxy to request a nonexistent resource which produces 404. The first and fastest fix is to confirm the value passed to the instances flag or the environment variable for the instance connection name exactly matches what is shown in the Cloud SQL console.

Enable the Cloud SQL Admin API in the Google Cloud project is not the first step because if the API were disabled you would see an API not enabled or a permission error rather than 404. A 404 points to a bad identifier rather than a disabled API.

Verify that the proxy is targeting the correct Google Cloud project in its configuration is not the best initial action because the proxy relies on the instance connection name and the credentials. If the project is wrong in the configuration it will also be wrong in the connection name which is exactly what you must correct first.

Grant the service account the Cloud SQL Client role would address authorization problems which typically present as 403 or authentication failures rather than 404. Since the symptom is 404 this is not the right first step.
originalQuery: You are troubleshooting a connection issue with a newly deployed Cloud SQL instance on Google Cloud. While investigating the Cloud SQL Proxy logs, you see the message Error 404: Not Found. What should you do?
originalOptions:
A. Ensure that you are using an internal (private) IP address interface.
B. Confirm that the instance connection name specified in your configuration is correct.
C. Check if the Cloud SQL Admin API is enabled.
D. Verify that your service account has the necessary IAM roles to connect to the Cloud SQL instance.
domain: Deploy scalable and highly available databases in Google Cloud
tip: When you see an error code from the Cloud SQL Auth Proxy map it to the most likely layer. A 404 usually means the instance connection name is wrong so verify the exact project region and instance ID string before changing IAM or APIs.

query: You are supporting a Cloud Spanner workload for a scooter rental startup named MetroScoot, where each trip is stored in a table named trip_ledger with trip_id and courier_id columns, and the application must retrieve trips for a specific courier within a caller supplied start and end date window, so which parameterized SQL statement should you use to make the query efficient and reusable?

options.text: SELECT * FROM trip_ledger WHERE courier_id LIKE @courierId AND trip_date>=@fromDate AND trip_date<=@toDate
options.explanation: This statement uses a LIKE comparison on the courier identifier while also applying parameterized lower and upper bounds for the date range

options.text: SELECT * FROM trip_ledger WHERE courier_id=@courierId AND trip_date BETWEEN '2022-02-01' AND '2022-02-28'
options.explanation: This statement mixes a parameter for the courier with hard coded literal dates for the time window

options.text: SELECT * FROM trip_ledger WHERE courier_id=@courierId AND trip_date BETWEEN @fromDate AND @toDate
options.explanation: This statement uses parameters for the courier and both date boundaries so the application can supply values at runtime

options.text: SELECT * FROM trip_ledger WHERE courier_id='dr-7788' AND trip_date BETWEEN @fromDate AND @toDate
options.explanation: This statement hard codes the courier identifier while parameterizing the date range

answer:
The correct option is SELECT * FROM trip_ledger WHERE courier_id=@courierId AND trip_date BETWEEN @fromDate AND @toDate because it uses named parameters for both the courier identifier and the start and end dates which makes the query reusable and it expresses the date window efficiently with an inclusive range.

This statement uses Cloud Spanner named parameters with the at symbol which allows the database to reuse query plans and helps avoid SQL injection. Using BETWEEN on the trip_date column matches a caller supplied start and end window in a single sargable predicate that can take advantage of indexing. Using equality on courier_id is appropriate for an exact courier lookup and is also index friendly.

SELECT * FROM trip_ledger WHERE courier_id LIKE @courierId AND trip_date>=@fromDate AND trip_date<=@toDate is not ideal because LIKE is intended for pattern matching and can disable efficient index use when wildcards are present. The requirement is an exact courier match so equality is preferable.

SELECT * FROM trip_ledger WHERE courier_id=@courierId AND trip_date BETWEEN '2022-02-01' AND '2022-02-28' hardcodes the date range which violates the requirement for a caller supplied window and reduces reusability. Parameters should be used for the dates to keep the query efficient and safe.

SELECT * FROM trip_ledger WHERE courier_id='dr-7788' AND trip_date BETWEEN @fromDate AND @toDate hardcodes the courier identifier which makes the statement unusable for other couriers and is not aligned with parameterization best practices.
originalQuery: As a Cloud Database Engineer, you are optimizing a Cloud Spanner database for a transportation company. Ride details are stored in a table with a rideId and driverId . The application needs to fetch ride information based on the driver and specific date ranges. You are tasked with creating an efficient, parameterized query. What should you do?
originalOptions:
A. SELECT * FROM rides WHERE driverId LIKE @driverId AND date>=@startDate AND date<=@endDate
B. SELECT * FROM rides WHERE driverId=@driverId AND date BETWEEN '2021-01-01' AND '2021-01-31'
C. SELECT * FROM rides WHERE driverId='driver123' AND date BETWEEN @startDate AND @endDate
D. SELECT * FROM rides WHERE driverId=@driverId AND date BETWEEN @startDate AND @endDate
domain: Design scalable and highly available cloud database solutions
tip: Look for parameterized queries that replace user provided values with named parameters and prefer equality for exact lookups and range predicates for date windows. Ask yourself whether the query would be easy to reuse across callers and whether the predicates are index friendly.

query: At BrightCrate Media you need to standardize how Cloud SQL instances are provisioned across 9 Google Cloud projects. Product teams must be able to request customizable builds, and the platform group requires strict adherence to organization policies and secure role based access with full auditability. What approach should you implement to satisfy these needs?

options.text: Manage Cloud SQL provisioning with Config Connector and Anthos Config Management and rely on Google Groups and folder policies for access control

query: You are the Cloud Database Engineer at Oriole Media and you must migrate a 12 TB on-premises MySQL 5.7 database into Cloud SQL for MySQL with less than 10 minutes of cutover downtime. answer:
The correct approach is Run Database Migration Service in continuous replication mode from the on-premises MySQL source into Cloud SQL for MySQL, validate the target, then perform a brief cutover.

Database Migration Service streams changes from the source using binlog replication which keeps the Cloud SQL target in near real time sync while the initial load completes. This enables a short cutover window that can meet the less than ten minute requirement. It also tolerates brief network interruptions because replication resumes from the last processed position without a full restart. With the target continuously updated, your team can validate data and run smoke tests before directing production traffic, then you perform the brief cutover when you are satisfied.

For a 12 TB database this approach is designed to handle large initial loads and keep pace with ongoing changes. It is supported for MySQL 5.7 sources migrating into Cloud SQL for MySQL and it provides a predictable and tested path for low downtime migrations.

answer:
The correct choice is Provision a Cloud Spanner regional instance with 4 nodes in a single region. This configuration delivers high availability within a region and supports horizontal scaling by adding nodes while keeping costs lower than multi-region deployments.

A regional instance replicates data across multiple zones within one region and provides automatic failover, which meets the high availability requirement for most workloads that do not need cross region redundancy. You can scale horizontally by increasing the number of nodes or processing units, and because all replicas are in one region the cost is significantly lower than a multi-region configuration.

Provision a Cloud Spanner multi-region instance with 4 nodes in each of 5 regions is unnecessary for the stated goals because multi-region is designed for cross region availability and comes with higher cost. Provision a Cloud Spanner multi-region instance and allocate 1 node in each of 5 regions would still incur the higher cost of multi-region and would provide limited throughput. It also misrepresents how capacity is specified because Spanner does not let you assign nodes to individual regions and minimum practical capacity for production multi-region workloads is higher than a single node per replica.

Provision a Cloud Spanner multi-region instance but place 1 node in a single region contradicts how multi-region configurations work. In multi-region, replicas are automatically distributed across regions defined by the instance configuration and you cannot concentrate capacity in only one region.

Parameterizing the passenger identifier improves performance because Spanner can cache and reuse the query plan for many different passengers while avoiding repeated compilation. The correct option is Build a fully mirrored environment in a separate Google Cloud project and stream changes from production in near real time, then run the disaster recovery drills there.

You can recreate the full three tier topology so that you validate the runbook end to end. By streaming changes in near real time you exercise with current data and system state which produces accurate RTO and RPO measurements without sending any customer requests to the test environment. Managed database services always use a flat monthly fee, while self managed databases are billed only when queries execute is wrong because pricing varies by product and is typically based on provisioned or consumed resources. Self managed databases incur costs for the virtual machines, storage, and networking while managed services charge for CPU, memory, storage, and operations rather than per query.
